scenes.visual: Title card 'A Clock Made of Cuts' over a TEAL chromosome with one ORANGE block. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: TEAL = Homo sapiens (modern humans); ORANGE = Neanderthal; PURPLE = Denisovan; GREY-GOLD = ash and dated layers, flints and date tags. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Skulls, maps and chromosomes are simple labelled cartoons; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Chromosome segment lengths in the line-up are schematic, ordered as in the lesson's table (Bacho Kiro: over 10 cM; Ust'-Ishim: about 0.2-0.4 cM; present day: about 0.05-0.07 cM).

scenes.tts: Fossils show where people lived, not who had children together. That needs DNA. If you carry Neanderthal DNA, when did it get there?
scenes.visual: Brief recap: the first film's checklist card 'What was dated? Where did it lie?' shrinks into a corner. A TEAL person silhouette appears with a small ORANGE fleck in its chest and a question tag 'when?'
scenes.narration: Fossils show where people lived, not who had children together. That needs DNA. If you carry Neanderthal DNA, when did it get there?

scenes.tts: Start with a clue. A draft Neanderthal genome was compared with genomes of living people. It shared more variants, sites where genomes differ, with sampled Eurasians than with sampled sub-Saharan Africans.
scenes.visual: Two stacks of small blocks grow side by side, labelled 'Eurasian + Neanderthal share' and 'African + Neanderthal share'. The first stack ends taller. Caption tag: 'Green et al., 2010'. Label 'schematic'. No formula on screen.
scenes.narration: Start with a clue. A draft Neanderthal genome was compared with genomes of living people. It shared more variants, sites where genomes differ, with sampled Eurasians than with sampled sub-Saharan Africans.

scenes.tts: The team read this as suggesting interbreeding after some people left Africa. But a clue is not proof, and it gives no date. An old African population, split into partly separate groups, could produce some of it.
scenes.visual: Over the taller stack a tag appears: 'a clue to mixing: not proof, no date'. A second, faded tag: 'or old population structure?'
scenes.narration: The team read this as suggesting interbreeding after some people left Africa. But a clue is not proof, and it gives no date. An old African population, split into partly separate groups, could produce some of it.

scenes.tts: So look along a chromosome instead. Picture one teal chromosome in a modern human. It carries one long orange block, inherited from a Neanderthal ancestor. At first the block is long and unbroken.
scenes.visual: The stacks slide away. A long horizontal TEAL chromosome bar fills the screen, with one long ORANGE block in its middle, labelled 'inherited from a Neanderthal ancestor'.
scenes.narration: So look along a chromosome instead. Picture one teal chromosome in a modern human. It carries one long orange block, inherited from a Neanderthal ancestor. At first the block is long and unbroken.

scenes.tts: Each time eggs and sperm are made, paired chromosomes swap pieces. This is recombination. A swap inside the orange block can split it, in the copy passed to a child.
scenes.visual: A second, all-TEAL chromosome lines up beneath. Small scissor marks appear at random points; at each cut the two bars swap the pieces beyond it. Some cuts fall outside the ORANGE block and leave it whole; one falls inside it, and part of the orange is replaced by teal in the copy passed on. Label 'recombination'.
scenes.narration: Each time eggs and sperm are made, paired chromosomes swap pieces. This is recombination. A swap inside the orange block can split it, in the copy passed to a child.

scenes.tts: Generation after generation, the swaps pile up. Some descendants keep the orange block whole. Some keep a shorter piece, and some lose it. Across many descendants, the orange pieces that survive get shorter on average.
scenes.visual: A generation counter in the corner ticks 1, 2, 5, 10, 100. The single chromosome branches into a panel of descendant chromosomes, one bar per descendant. On each bar the original ORANGE block is kept whole, cut shorter, or gone (all TEAL). As the counter rises, the surviving ORANGE blocks across the panel get shorter on average. No single bar breaks one block into scattered islands; if a genome shows several separate ORANGE tracts, a small tag reads 'from different ancestral copies'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Generation after generation, the swaps pile up. Some descendants keep the orange block whole. Some keep a shorter piece, and some lose it. Across many descendants, the orange pieces that survive get shorter on average.

scenes.tts: That makes length a clock. Long orange segments mean the mixing happened recently. Short flecks mean it happened long ago.
scenes.visual: The counter becomes a clock face. Beside it, two small chromosomes: one with a long ORANGE run tagged 'recent', one with tiny ORANGE flecks tagged 'long ago'.
scenes.narration: That makes length a clock. Long orange segments mean the mixing happened recently. Short flecks mean it happened long ago.

scenes.tts: Today, after far more generations, the Neanderthal pieces in living non-Africans are short. The cutting has run a long time.
scenes.visual: A chromosome labelled 'present-day non-African' with scattered tiny ORANGE flecks. On screen: '~1,500-2,000 generations (model-based)' and 'average ~0.05-0.07 cM'.
scenes.narration: Today, after far more generations, the Neanderthal pieces in living non-Africans are short. The cutting has run a long time.

scenes.tts: Now meet Oost-Ishim, a man who lived in western Siberia long before us. Will his orange segments be longer or shorter than yours?
scenes.caption: Now meet Ust'-Ishim, a man who lived in western Siberia long before us. Will his orange segments be longer or shorter than yours?
scenes.visual: A pin on western Siberia, 'Ust'-Ishim, ~45,000 years ago', with a TEAL figure. His chromosome appears above the present-day one, but its ORANGE pieces are hidden behind a question mark. Two choices: 'longer?' 'shorter?'
scenes.narration: Now meet Ust'-Ishim, a man who lived in western Siberia long before us. Will his orange segments be longer or shorter than yours?

scenes.visual: Hold on the hidden chromosome and the two choices; a timer ring fills over five seconds.

scenes.tts: Longer. Fewer generations of cutting had passed since the mixing. From their lengths, Fu and colleagues worked out how long before his life the gene flow came.
scenes.visual: The question mark lifts: his chromosome shows medium ORANGE pieces, clearly longer than the present-day flecks below. On screen: '232-430 generations (single-pulse fit)', 'gene flow 7,000-13,000 years before him (Fu et al., 2014)'. 'longer?' turns TEAL with a tick.
scenes.narration: Longer. Fewer generations of cutting had passed since the mixing. From their lengths, Fu and colleagues worked out how long before his life the gene flow came.

scenes.tts: At Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, three early Homo sapiens were sampled. Each had a Neanderthal ancestor only a few generations back. That was a separate, recent contact in their own family trees. Their orange runs are the longest of all.
scenes.visual: A pin on Bulgaria, 'Bacho Kiro Cave', three TEAL figures, each with a small family tree whose top branch, a few generations up, is ORANGE. Their chromosome shows very long ORANGE runs plus a few short flecks. On screen: 'about 7 generations or fewer', 'longest segments 17-54 cM', 'a separate, recent contact' (Hajdinjak et al., 2021).
scenes.narration: At Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, three early Homo sapiens were sampled. Each had a Neanderthal ancestor only a few generations back. That was a separate, recent contact in their own family trees. Their orange runs are the longest of all.

scenes.tts: Line the three up. Bacho Kiro, long runs. Oost-Ishim, medium pieces. A living person, short flecks. The surplus was a clue. The lengths test it, and say when.
scenes.caption: Line the three up. Bacho Kiro, long runs. Ust'-Ishim, medium pieces. A living person, short flecks. The surplus was a clue. The lengths test it, and say when.
scenes.visual: Three chromosomes stacked top to bottom: Bacho Kiro (long ORANGE runs, tagged 'separate recent contact'), Ust'-Ishim (medium pieces), present day (short flecks). A generation axis on the left: 'about 7 or fewer', '232-430', '~1,500-2,000'. Label 'schematic lengths'. The two-stack clue appears small beside them, tagged 'clue', and the line-up is tagged 'test and date'.
scenes.narration: Line the three up. Bacho Kiro, long runs. Ust'-Ishim, medium pieces. A living person, short flecks. The surplus was a clue. The lengths test it, and say when.

scenes.tts: One caution travels with this clock. It gives an average, for one main period of mixing. And it says when, not how much ancestry came across.
scenes.visual: A small scope card slides over the line-up: 'average', 'one main period of mixing', 'when, not how much'.
scenes.narration: One caution travels with this clock. It gives an average, for one main period of mixing. And it says when, not how much ancestry came across.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Line: 'Long segments mean recent mixing: length is the clock.'
